metadata.title: Using machine learning to improve Q-matrix validation

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The empirical illustration uses a sub-dataset of PISA 2000 reading for German students (1095 students) with non-missing dichotomized responses; the manuscript does not describe any complex survey weighting variables or replicate-weight procedures for this analysis. Because the study’s main contribution is methodological (simulation-based training of ML classifiers on simulated Q-matrix features) and the real-data section focuses on Q-matrix validation using G-DINA fit indices, the paper does not report applying PISA sampling weights (e.g., student/school weights) or any BRR/jackknife replication. The ML models (random forest and feed-forward neural networks) are trained and evaluated on simulated datasets and then used to suggest Q-matrix modifications; the paper does not document weight-aware estimation. Therefore, weighting strategy is not specified and should be treated as unreported/omitted for the empirical subset.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variable is not an ILSA cognitive achievement score generated via PVs; instead, the study validates cognitive-diagnostic Q-matrices by classifying item q-vectors (and evaluates Q-matrix recovery/fit) using PVAF and McFadden pseudo-R2 as features. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper only states that the real-data subset consists of non-missing dichotomized responses, but it does not describe any additional missingness rules for the ML training inputs or simulation-to-real-data mapping. This is a reporting gap for transparency about how any remaining missingness (e.g., in derived fit indices or intermediate computations) would be handled.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Real-data analysis uses a sub-dataset of PISA 2000 reading for German students containing 20 reading items (Booklets 8 and 9) and includes only non-missing dichotomized responses; the manuscript does not specify further exclusions beyond non-missing response availability. The simulation studies generate synthetic datasets under controlled conditions (e.g., K=3/5/7 attributes, N sampled from U(400,800) in training-data generation; 70% training / 30% testing), so no country filtering applies to simulations.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2000 Reading (German students; 20 items from Booklets 8 & 9)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Real-data fit statistics: RF-P suggested Q-matrix had best absolute/relative fit—M2 test p=.428 (adequate fit), RMSEA2=0.004 (smallest), and smallest SRSMR among comparable models; Table 9 also reports deviance=23,735.33, AIC=24,021.33, BIC=24,736.11. FNN-P and FNN-R could not compute M2/RMSEA2 due to too-low degrees of freedom; Hull and GDI had worse M2 p-values (M2 p=.011 and .000) and larger RMSEA2 (0.020 and 0.027).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2000 Reading data (German students; 20 dichotomized items) the study leveraged PVAF- and pseudo-R2-derived features to classify item q-vectors and thereby suggest validated Q-matrix modifications, finding that the Random Forest model using PVAF (RF-P) produced the best model–data fit (e.g., RMSEA2=0.004 and M2 test p=.428). This indicates that PVAF-informed random-forest Q-matrix validation can outperform established GDI and Hull procedures in practice, supporting a workflow where ML supplies auxiliary candidate Q-matrix entries for domain-expert review rather than replacing expert judgment.

main_findings.dataset_used: Simulation Study I (G-DINA-based synthetic Q-matrix data; K=3/5/7)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Across conditions in Study I, GDI had significantly lower QRR than the other five methods (ANOVA with Bonferroni; minimum QRR difference between GDI and others being 0.14, p<.001). For K=3 under higher-order attribute distribution, average QRR: RF-P=0.927, RF-R=0.924, FNN-P=0.923, FNN-R=0.920 vs GDI=0.914 and Hull=0.891. For K=5 under higher-order distribution, example metric values (test evaluation of MLMs): RF-P accuracy=0.708, F1=0.674, kappa=0.696; RF-R accuracy=0.728, F1=0.696, kappa=0.717; FNN-P accuracy=0.688, F1=0.654, kappa=0.676; FNN-R accuracy=0.729, F1=0.701, kappa=0.718. For K=7, RF-R had higher accuracy (0.607) than RF-P, FNN-P, FNN-R (0.553, 0.552, 0.591).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using simulation data generated under the G-DINA framework (varying K, item quality, misspecification rate, attribute distribution, N, and JK), the study leveraged ML classifiers trained on PVAF or McFadden pseudo-R2 features to predict the correct item q-vectors, finding that the ML-based validation methods achieved higher Q-matrix recovery rates than GDI and Hull in most conditions (e.g., for K=3, QRR≈0.927 for RF-P vs 0.891 for Hull). This indicates that ML-based Q-matrix validation can reduce the need for fixed PVAF cutoffs and improve robustness across data conditions, though the results are based on simulated recovery metrics rather than causal effects on examinee classification.

main_findings.dataset_used: Simulation Study II (G-DINA-based synthetic Q-matrix data; robustness conditions)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Study II ANOVA with Bonferroni: GDI QRR significantly lower than other five methods (p<.001; minimum difference 0.148). No significant differences among the four MLMs and Hull, but RF-P had the highest QRR averages. Under higher-order attribute distribution: when K=3, QRR averages RF-P=0.918, RF-R=0.915, FNN-P=0.917, FNN-R=0.915 vs Hull=0.871; when K=5, GDI was lowest (0.785). Robustness to sample size: compared to N=200, QRR increased by about 9–10% for MLMs at N=1000 and by about 9.6–10.2% at N=1500 (reported as RF-P 9.06%/9.68%, RF-R 9.07%/9.60%, FNN-P 9.36%/10.22%, FNN-R 9.46%/10.23%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using simulation data with robustness conditions different from the MLM training setup (wider N and JK ranges and simpler Q-matrix structures), the study leveraged PVAF- and pseudo-R2-based ML classifiers to validate Q-matrices, finding that the ML-based methods maintained competitive or superior QRR relative to Hull and clearly outperformed GDI (e.g., K=3 QRR≈0.918 for RF-P vs 0.871 for Hull). This indicates that ML-based Q-matrix validation is feasible and relatively robust to changes in data conditions, supporting its use as an auxiliary validation tool for domain experts when empirical Q-matrix misspecification is expected.

data.outcome_summary: This paper proposes four ML-based Q-matrix validation methods for cognitive diagnostic models, using random forest and feed-forward neural networks trained on features derived from PVAF and McFadden pseudo-R2. Because the task is Q-matrix validation (classifying item q-vectors) rather than predicting PV-based achievement, plausible values are not part of the outcome. In two simulation studies under a G-DINA data-generating process, the ML-based methods achieved higher Q-matrix recovery rates than the GDI and generally outperformed the Hull method, with RF-P showing the highest average QRR across both studies. In a real-data illustration using a PISA 2000 reading sub-dataset for German students (20 items; 1095 students), the RF-P suggested Q-matrix showed the best fit (M2 test p=.428 and RMSEA2=0.004), while FNN-based suggestions could not compute some fit indices due to low degrees of freedom. A key limitation is that the empirical analysis does not report survey-weighting or missing-data handling beyond stating non-missing dichotomized responses, and the ML is used to assist expert review rather than to establish causal correctness of attribute-item mappings.
